title: parousia
summary: The references connect expectation of Christ’s coming with resurrection and renewed creation. Daniel 12 depicts awakening from death; 1 Corinthians 15 discusses Christ’s reign and the raising of the dead; 1 Thessalonians 4 addresses the coming of the Lord and comfort for mourners; Revelation 21 pictures a world without death or grief. The passages share a future hope, but they do not all describe the same event in the same terms or provide a complete timetable.
historical_context: The set combines Daniel’s apocalyptic vision, Paul’s letters to communities, and Revelation’s vision. The references support this comparison of textual settings; they do not provide independent evidence for detailed chronology or for the history of the Greek term.
canonical_context: Paul’s letters connect the Lord’s coming with resurrection and the community’s hope; Daniel provides a vision of awakening; Revelation concludes with the removal of death and grief. These texts fit a broad canonical hope for God’s future action, while each has a distinct literary purpose.
literary_context: Daniel and Revelation present visions; 1 Corinthians argues about resurrection and reign; 1 Thessalonians gives pastoral reassurance. A vision, theological argument, and letter to grieving readers should not be converted into one chronological chart. The shared theme is expectation, not identical wording or detail.
covenantal_significance: The passages encourage hope that death does not have the final word and that God will complete the work associated with Christ’s reign. They connect coming, resurrection, and renewal without defining every step or resolving interpretive differences not documented in this entry.
canonical_role: This entry gathers passages about expectation, resurrection, and renewal. It shows how Paul’s pastoral teaching relates to Daniel’s and Revelation’s visions without claiming that the selected texts supply a complete sequence of end-time events.
